claim: The human brain supports social cognitive functions, including Theory of Mind, empathy, and compassion, through its intrinsic hierarchical organization.
source: The human brain supports social cognitive functions, including Theory of Mind, empathy, and compassion, through its intrinsic hierarchical organization.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain organization and social cognition, drawing on established scientific knowledge about brain function.

claim: 332 healthy adults (197 women, 20–55 years) participated in the study with repeated multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing.
source: We studied if different types of social mental training induce changes in cortical function and microstructure, investigating 332 healthy adults (197 women, 20–55 years) with repeated multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample size and demographics.

claim: Cortical function and microstructure changed as a result of attention-mindfulness and socio-cognitive training in regions functionally associated with attention and interoception, including insular and parietal cortices.
source: In particular, cortical function and microstructure changed as a result of attention-mindfulness and socio-cognitive training in regions functionally associated with attention and interoception, including insular and parietal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the longitudinal neuroimaging study.

claim: Socio-affective and socio-cognitive training resulted in differential microstructural changes in regions classically implicated in interoceptive and emotional processing, including insular and orbitofrontal areas, but did not result in functional reorganization.
source: Conversely, socio-affective and socio-cognitive training resulted in differential microstructural changes in regions classically implicated in interoceptive and emotional processing, including insular and orbitofrontal areas, but did not result in functional reorganization.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing different training modules.

claim: Longitudinal changes in cortical function and microstructure predicted behavioral change in attention, compassion and perspective-taking.
source: Notably, longitudinal changes in cortical function and microstructure predicted behavioral change in attention, compassion and perspective-taking.
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analyses using cross-validation.

claim: Social capacities can be divided into socio-affective abilities (such as empathy and compassion) and socio-cognitive abilities (such as Theory of Mind or mentalizing).
source: Social capacities can be divided into multiple sub-components (Singer, 2006; Schurz et al., 2020; Schurz et al., 2021): (i) socio-affective (or emotional-motivational) abilities such as empathy allowing us to share feelings with others, and may give rise to compassion and prosocial motivation (Batson, 2009; Eisenberg and Fabes, 1990; de Vignemont and Singer, 2006); (ii) socio-cognitive abilities gain access to beliefs and intentions of others [also referred to as Theory of Mind (ToM) or mentalizing (Singer, 2006; Frith and Frith, 2006; Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003)].
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Tasks probing socio-emotional functioning and empathy consistently elicit functional activations in anterior insula, supramarginal gyrus, and midcingulate cortex.
source: For example, tasks probing socio-emotional functioning and empathy consistently elicit functional activations in anterior insula, supramarginal gyrus, and midcingulate cortex (Singer, 2006; Singer and Lamm, 2009; Singer et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional neuroimaging studies.

claim: Tasks involving socio-cognitive functioning generally activate regions of the human default mode network, such as medial frontal cortex, temporo-parietal junction, and superior temporal sulcus.
source: On the other hand, tasks involving socio-cognitive functioning generally activate regions of the human default mode network (DMN), such as medial frontal cortex, temporo-parietal junction, and superior temporal sulcus (Schurz et al., 2020; Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003; Bzdok et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional neuroimaging studies.

claim: Attentional tasks activate inferior parietal and lateral frontal and anterior insular cortices.
source: Finally, attentional tasks activate inferior parietal and lateral frontal and anterior insular cortices (Trautwein et al., 2016; Corbetta et al., 2008; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional neuroimaging studies.

claim: Interoceptive awareness is linked to anterior insula and cingulate regions.
source: and interoceptive awareness is linked to anterior insula and cingulate regions (Craig, 2009; Kleckner et al., 2017; Seth and Friston, 2016; Critchley et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical function and microstructure follow parallel spatial patterns, notably a sensory-transmodal axis that may support the differentiation of sensory and motor function from higher order cognitive processes, such as social cognition.
source: Prior research has shown that cortical function and microstructure follow parallel spatial patterns, notably a sensory-transmodal axis that may support the differentiation of sensory and motor function from higher order cognitive processes, such as social cognition (Valk et al., 2022; Park et al., 2021b; Paquola et al., 2019b; Huntenburg et al., 2017; Goulas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cortical organization.

claim: Mental training may alter brain function and gross morphology.
source: A range of prior studies indicated that mental training may alter brain function and gross morphology (Slagter et al., 2007; Hölzel et al., 2011; Lazar et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2016; Fox et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on mental training effects.

claim: A randomized controlled trial showed little effect on brain morphology of 8 weeks of mindfulness-based training in healthy adults.
source: For example, a randomized controlled trial showed little effect on brain morphology of 8 weeks of mindfulness-based training in healthy adults (Kral et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific randomized controlled trial.

claim: The ReSource project demonstrated differentiable change in MRI-derived cortical thickness, in support of macrostructural plasticity of the adult brain following the training of social and interoceptive skills.
source: In a previous study realized in the context of the ReSource project (Singer et al., 2016), our group demonstrated differentiable change in MRI-derived cortical thickness, in support of macrostructural plasticity of the adult brain following the training of social and interoceptive skills (Valk et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study from the same research group.

claim: The ReSource project involved a targeted training of attention-mindfulness (Presence training-module), followed by socio-affective (Affect TM) and socio-cognitive/ToM training (Perspective TM) over the course of nine months.
source: As the ReSource project involved a targeted training of attention-mindfulness (Presence training-module, TM), followed by socio-affective (Affect TM) and socio-cognitive/ToM training (Perspective TM) over the course of nine months, this study design can help to dissociate different mental training effects.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: The first three functional gradients explain in total more than 50% of variance within the functional connectome.
source: To investigate changes in intrinsic functional organization following different types of social and cognitive mental training we focused on changes within a 3D framework of functional axes, explaining in total more than 50% of variance within the functional connectome (Margulies et al., 2016; de Wael et al., 2020; Coifman et al., 2005; Haak and Beckmann, 2020; Bernhardt et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on functional gradients.

claim: The a-priori networks showed a unique embedding in 3D gradient space (F(5,394) 8.727, P<0.001), with Affect-associated networks being most integrated while and Perspective-networks were most segregated.
source: Notably, the a-priori networks showed a unique embedding in 3D gradient space (F(5,394) 8.727, P<0.001), with Affect-associated networks being most integrated while and Perspective-networks were most segregated.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the baseline data.

claim: Presence training resulted in increased eccentricity of bilateral temporal and right superior parietal areas (FDRq <0.05), indicative of increased segregation.
source: Presence training resulted in increased eccentricity of bilateral temporal and right superior parietal areas (FDRq <0.05), indicative of increased segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of longitudinal neuroimaging data.

claim: Perspective training resulted in decreased eccentricity of right temporal regions, together with left insular cortices (FDRq <0.05).
source: Perspective training resulted in decreased eccentricity of right temporal regions, together with left insular cortices (FDRq <0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of longitudinal neuroimaging data.

claim: No eccentricity change was observed following Affect training.
source: We observed no eccentricity change following Affect training.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis of longitudinal neuroimaging data.

claim: Changes between Presence and Perspective were most marked in G2 (t=–4.647, p<0.001, d=−0.403), dissociating sensory-motor from visual systems.
source: Post-hoc analysis indicated changes between Presence and Perspective were underlying eccentricity change were most marked in G2 (t=–4.647, p<0.001, d=−0.403), dissociating sensory-motor from visual systems, but not G1 (t=–1.495, p>0.05, d=−0.130) or G3 (t=–0.493, p>0.05, d=−0.043) gradient.
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of the gradient data.

claim: Attention (t=2.842, p=0.005, d=0.247) and interoception (t=2.765, p=0.006, d=0.240) networks showed alterations in Presence-vs-Perspective.
source: Focussing on a-priori networks, in particular attention (t=2.842, p=0.005, d=0.247) and interoception (t=2.765, p=0.006, d=0.240) networks showed alterations in Presence-vs-Perspective, (Table 4, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of a-priori network changes.

claim: Overall, ReSource training led to decreased qT1 values, i.e. increased myelination, in both TC1 and TC2 relative to RCC over the nine months training time, in all a-priori functional networks in particular in deeper compartment microstructure.
source: Overall, ReSource training led to decreased qT1 values, i.e. increased myelination, in both TC1 and TC2 relative to RCC over the nine months training time, in all a-priori functional networks in particular in deeper compartment microstructure, whereas RCC showed subtle increases of qT1, suggesting decreased myelination (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1p, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal analysis of qT1 data.

claim: Presence showed marked increases in qT1 in posterior areas in superficial depth compartments, and marked decreases in qT1 in prefrontal and occipital regions that showed increased spatial extent as a function of cortical depth.
source: Presence showed marked increases in qT1 in posterior areas in superficial depth compartments, and marked decreases in qT1 in prefrontal and occipital regions that showed increased spatial extent as a function of cortical depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by depth-dependent analysis of qT1 changes.

claim: Affect resulted in extended decreases in qT1 in mid and deep depth compartments, in particular in bilateral frontal areas extending to parietal lobe, bilateral posterior cingulate, left fusiform gyrus and right insula.
source: Conversely, Affect resulted in extended decreases in qT1 in mid and deep depth compartments, in particular in bilateral frontal areas extending to parietal lobe, bilateral posterior cingulate, left fusiform gyrus and right insula.
evidence: This claim is supported by depth-dependent analysis of qT1 changes.

claim: Perspective showed largely decreases in qT1 in superficial depths in parietal-temporal, precuneus, and sensory-motor areas, and an increase in qT1 in left prefrontal regions.
source: Perspective showed largely decreases in qT1 in superficial depths in parietal-temporal, precuneus, and sensory-motor areas, and an increase in qT1 in left prefrontal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by depth-dependent analysis of qT1 changes.

claim: A correspondence (FDRq <0.05) was observed between functional eccentricity and upper layer microstructural compartments (1st: t=3.167 p=0.002, d=0.275; 2nd compartment: t=2.911, p=0.004, d=0.253) in regions showing differences in eccentricity between Presence and Perspective.
source: We observed a correspondence (FDRq <0.05) between functional eccentricity and upper layer microstructural compartments (1st: t=3.167 p=0.002, d=0.275; 2nd compartment: t=2.911, p=0.004, d=0.253) in regions showing differences in eccentricity between Presence and Perspective.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis correlating functional and microstructural changes.

claim: All but the emotion network showed increases in qT1 of Presence versus Affect and Perspective in the upper compartments, extending to deeper compartments when comparing Presence and Affect (FDRq <0.05).
source: Following, assessing TM-specific effects in microstructure in a-priori task-based functional networks through comparing all TMs, we found all but the emotion network to show increases in qT1 of Presence versus Affect and Perspective in the upper compartments, extending to deeper compartments when comparing Presence and Affect (FDRq <0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of network-specific microstructural changes.

claim: Decreases of Affect relative to Perspective were observed in deeper compartments, near the GM/WM boundary, in interoception and emotion-related networks.
source: Conversely, in deeper compartments, near the GM/WM boundary, we observed decreases of Affect relative to Perspective in interoception and emotion-related networks
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of depth-dependent microstructural changes.

claim: A spatial correlation was observed between functional change in eccentricity and G2 in upper and middle compartment microstructure in Presence and overall correspondence with G3 changes, correcting for spatial autocorrelation (pspin <0.05).
source: Exploring correspondence between functional and microstructural change within TMs, rather than by contrasting TMs, we observed a spatial correlation between functional change in eccentricity and G2 in upper and middle compartment microstructure in Presence and overall correspondence with G3 changes, correcting for spatial autocorrelation (pspin <0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis with correction for spatial autocorrelation.

claim: Microstructural alterations in mid- and deeper compartments showed correspondence to eccentricity and G2 in Affect (pspin <0.05).
source: whereas microstructural alterations in mid- and deeper compartments showed correspondence to eccentricity and G2 in Affect (pspin <0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis with correction for spatial autocorrelation.

claim: Attention change predictions in Presence (N=85, TC1 and TC2) were most marked in attention network in microstructure at superficial depths and eccentricity (nMAE (mean ± SD): –0.037±0.003, out of sample r (mean ± SD): 0.325±0.308).
source: Attention change predictions in Presence (N=85, TC1 and TC2) were most marked in attention network in microstructure at superficial depts and eccentricity (nMAE (mean ± SD): –0.037±0.003, out of sample r (mean ± SD): 0.325±0.308).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analysis with cross-validation.

claim: Compassion change following Affect (N=100, TC1 and TC2) was predicted primarily through structural and functional reorganization of attention, interoception and emotion networks (MAE: –0.412±0.029, out of sample r: 0.284±0.279).
source: Conversely, compassion change following Affect (N=100, TC1 and TC2) was predicted primarily through structural and functional reorganization of attention, interoception and emotion networks (MAE: –0.412±0.029, out of sample r: 0.284±0.279).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analysis with cross-validation.

claim: Theory of Mind change following Perspective (N=93, TC1 and TC2) predictions (nMAE: –0.081±0.006 out-of-sample r: 0.301±0.281) were most likely to occur in attention networks along G3 and microstructure of upper and middle compartments, as well as emotion related networks along G3.
source: Last, Theory of Mind change following Perspective (N=93, TC1 and TC2) predictions (nMAE: –0.081±0.006 out-of-sample r: 0.301±0.281) were most likely to occur in attention networks along G3 and microstructure of upper and middle compartments, as well as emotion related networks along G3.
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning prediction analysis with cross-validation.

claim: In all cases, the domain-specific TM model performed best on test data of the respective TM (p<0.001).
source: We found that in all cases, the domain-specific TM model performed best on test data of the respective TM (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of prediction model performance.

claim: Integrated states might reflect active thought processes such as those required when engaging in ToM, while more segregated states may reflect automation and domain-specific function.
source: In the context of social cognition, integrated states might reflect active thought processes such as those required when engaging in ToM, while more segregated states may reflect automation and domain-specific function (Finc et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The lack of change in eccentricity following socio-affective training reflects a coordinating role of socio-affect relative to alterations associated with attention-mindfulness and socio-cognition.
source: It is possible that the lack of change in eccentricity following socio-affective training reflects a coordinating role of socio-affect relative to alterations associated with attention-mindfulness and socio-cognition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Affective processing may balance integration and segregation of brain function to regulate resources dynamically.
source: Such an interpretation aligns with theories of emotional allostasis, suggesting that affective processing may balance integration and segregation of brain function to regulate resources dynamically (Chun et al., 2011; Barrett, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Socio-cognitive training resulted in increased myelination proxy (reflected by decreases in qT1) values in attention and interoception networks, whereas attention-based mindfulness training resulted in decreased myelination of these regions.
source: Whereas socio-cognitive training resulted in increased myelination proxy (reflected by decreases in qT1) values, attention-based mindfulness training resulted in decreased myelination of these regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of qT1 data in specific networks.

claim: Social isolation during development resulted in changes in mPFC myelination, correlating with working memory and social behaviors in mice.
source: Work in mice has shown that social isolation during development resulted in changes in mPFC myelination, correlating with working memory and social behaviors (Makinodan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior animal study.

claim: The observed alterations in qT1 may reflect changes in oligodendrites as well as supporting glial cells.
source: The observed alterations in qT1 in our study may reflect changes in oligodendrites as well as supporting glial cells (Bonetto et al., 2020; Chorghay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the qT1 findings supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Myelin-plasticity has been suggested to be a key biological marker of learning and memory in adulthood.
source: Indeed, myelin-plasticity has been suggested to be a key biological marker of learning and memory in adulthood (de Faria et al., 2021; Xin and Chan, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on myelin plasticity.

claim: Alterations persisted above and beyond cortical thickness change alone.
source: Interestingly, alterations persisted above and beyond cortical thickness change alone (Valk et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis controlling for cortical thickness.

claim: Ascending connections have been associated with middle cortical layers (origin: layer 3, termination: layer 4), while descending connectivity links to superficial and deeper layers (origin: layer 2, 3 A and 6, termination: layer 1 and 6).
source: Whereas ascending connections have been associated with middle cortical layers (origin: layer 3, termination: layer 4), descending connectivity links to superficial and deeper layers (origin: layer 2, 3 A and 6, termination: layer 1 and 6) (Bastos et al., 2012; Rockland, 2019; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cortical connectivity.

claim: Superficial layers of the transmodal cortex have been implicated in manipulating information, whereas deeper layers may have a more controlling function in humans.
source: Functionally, it has been suggested that, in humans, superficial layers of the transmodal cortex have been implicated in manipulating information, whereas deeper layers may have a more controlling function (Bastos et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on layer-specific function.

claim: Frontal regions dominate feedback processes, whereas parietal regions support feedforward functions.
source: Interestingly, using high-resolution data it has been shown that frontal regions dominate feedback processes, whereas parietal regions support feedforward functions (Huber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior high-resolution imaging study.

claim: Various studies in non-human mammals have indicated differential mechanisms of plasticity correspond to different layer-depths.
source: Moreover, various studies in non-human mammals have indicated differential mechanisms of plasticity correspond to different layer-depths (Verhoog et al., 2016; Goel and Lee, 2007; Yang et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: The study used a proxy of layer-depth that does not correspond to actual cortical layers, but rather creates depth-varying profiles of 1 mm resolution quantitative qT1 through interpolation.
source: It is of note that the current study used a proxy of layer-depth that does not correspond to actual cortical layers, but rather creates depth-varying profiles of 1 mm resolution quantitative qT1 though interpolation.
evidence: This is a methodological description and limitation of the study.

claim: Mental TMs focusing on attention, socio-emotional and socio-cognitive skills resulted in differentiable change in intrinsic functional and microstructural organization.
source: In sum, combining a longitudinal mental training study with multi-modal imaging, we could show that mental TMs focusing on attention, socio-emotional and socio-cognitive skills resulted in differentiable change in intrinsic functional and microstructural organization.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The findings are compatible with previous work suggesting a link between anatomical and functional hierarchies and global workspace theories of cognition.
source: As such, our findings are compatible with previous work suggesting a link between anatomical and functional hierarchies and global workspace theories of cognition (Dehaene et al., 1998; Baars, 2002; Deco et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: Targeted mental training can enhance social skills and lead to co-occurring reconfigurations of cortical function and microstructure, providing evidence for experience-dependent plasticity.
source: Although our work focused on healthy adults ranging from 20 to 55 years of age, our findings overall support the possibility that targeted mental training can enhance social skills and lead to co-occurring reconfigurations of cortical function and microstructure, providing evidence for experience-dependent plasticity.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretation of the study findings.

claim: A total of 332 healthy adults (197 women, mean ± SD = 40.7±9.2 years, 20–55 years), recruited in 2012–2014 participated in the study.
source: A total of 332 healthy adults (197 women, mean ± SD = 40.7±9.2 years, 20–55 years), recruited in 2012–2014 participated in the study, see Table 1 for more details.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: More than 95% of the sample was Caucasian, with catchment areas balanced across two German municipalities (Berlin and Leipzig).
source: More than 95% of our sample was Caucasian, with catchment areas balanced across two German municipalities (Berlin and Leipzig).
evidence: This is a demographic description of the study sample.

claim: Participants were excluded if they fulfilled criteria for an Axis-I disorder within the past two years or Schizophrenia, psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, substance dependency, or an Axis-II disorder at any time in their life.
source: Participants were excluded if they fulfilled criteria for: (i) an Axis-I disorder within the past two years; (ii) Schizophrenia, psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, substance dependency, or an Axis-II disorder at any time in their life.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committees of the University of Leipzig (#376/12-ff) and Humboldt University in Berlin (#2013–02, 2013–29, 2014–10).
source: All participants gave written informed consent and the study was approved by the Research Ethics Committees of the University of Leipzig (#376/12-ff) and Humboldt University in Berlin (#2013–02, 2013–29, 2014–10).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval of the study.

claim: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under the title 'Plasticity of the Compassionate Brain' (#NCT01833104).
source: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under the title 'Plasticity of the Compassionate Brain' (#NCT01833104).
evidence: This is a statement about study registration.

claim: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Verio using a 32-channel head coil.
source: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Verio (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) using a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Task-free functional MRI was recorded using a T2*-weighted gradient 2D-EPI sequence (repetition time [TR]=2000ms, echo time [TE]=27ms, flip angle = 90°; 37 slices tilted at approximately 30° with 3 mm slice thickness, field of view [FOV]=210 × 210mm2, matrix = 70 × 70, 3×3 × 3 mm3 voxels, 1 mm gap; 210 volumes per session).
source: We recorded task-free functional MRI using a T2*-weighted gradient 2D-EPI sequence (repetition time [TR]=2000ms, echo time [TE]=27ms, flip angle = 90°; 37 slices tilted at approximately 30° with 3 mm slice thickness, field of view [FOV]=210 × 210mm2, matrix = 70 × 70, 3×3 × 3 mm3 voxels, 1 mm gap; 210 volumes per session).
evidence: This is a description of the functional MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: A T1-weighted 3D-MPRAGE sequence was acquired (176 sagittal slices, TR = 2300ms, TE = 2.98ms, inversion time [TI]=900ms, flip angle = 7°, FOV = 240 × 256 mm2, matrix = 240 × 256, 1×1 × 1 mm3 voxels).
source: We also acquired a T1-weighted 3D-MPRAGE sequence (176 sagittal slices, TR = 2300ms, TE = 2.98ms, inversion time [TI]=900ms, flip angle = 7°, FOV = 240 × 256 mm2, matrix = 240 × 256, 1×1 × 1 mm3 voxels).
evidence: This is a description of the structural MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: For qT1 mapping, the 3D MP2RAGE sequence was used (Marques et al., 2010), which combines two MPRAGE datasets acquired at different inversion times to provide intrinsic bias field cancellation and estimation of T1 TR = 5000ms, TE = 2.89ms, TI = 700/2500ms, flip angle = 4/5°, FOV = 256 × 256 mm2, 1×1 × 1–mm3 voxels.
source: For qT1 mapping, we used the recently introduced 3D MP2RAGE sequence (Marques et al., 2010), which combines two MPRAGE datasets acquired at different inversion times to provide intrinsic bias field cancellation and estimation of T1 TR = 5000ms, TE = 2.89ms, TI = 700/2500ms, flip angle = 4/5°, FOV = 256 × 256 mm2, 1×1 × 1–mm3 voxels.
evidence: This is a description of the qT1 mapping acquisition parameters.

claim: The first 5 volumes were discarded to ensure steady-state magnetization.
source: We discarded the first 5 volumes to ensure steady-state magnetization, performed slice-time correction, motion correction and realignment, and co-registered functional time series of a given subject to the corresponding T1-weighted MRI.
evidence: This is a description of the fMRI preprocessing steps.

claim: Diffusion map embedding, a nonlinear manifold learning technique, identified principal gradient components, explaining functional connectivity variance in descending order.
source: Diffusion map embedding, a nonlinear manifold learning technique (Coifman et al., 2005), identified principal gradient components, explaining functional connectivity variance in descending order.
evidence: This is a description of the gradient analysis method.

claim: Individual embedding solutions were aligned to the group-level embedding based on the Human Connectome Project S1200 sample via Procrustes rotations.
source: Individual embedding solutions were aligned to the group-level embedding based on the Human Connectome Project S1200 sample (Van Essen et al., 2013) via Procrustes rotations (de Wael et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the gradient alignment method.

claim: T1-weighted MRIs were processed using FreeSurfer version 5.1.0 to generate cortical surface models for measurements of cortical thickness and surface area.
source: T1-weighted MRIs were processed using FreeSurfer (http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu) version 5.1.0 to generate cortical surface models for measurements of cortical thickness and surface area.
evidence: This is a description of the structural MRI processing method.

claim: FreeSurfer has been validated against histological analysis and manual measurements.
source: FreeSurfer has been validated against histological analysis (Rosas et al., 2002) and manual measurements (Kuperberg et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to validation studies.

claim: 12 equivolumetric surfaces were generated between outer and inner cortical surfaces.
source: We generated 12 equivolumetric surfaces between outer and inner cortical surfaces.
evidence: This is a description of the depth-dependent microstructure analysis method.

claim: The NeuroSynth meta-analytic database was used to assess topic terms associated with the training ('attention', 'interoception', 'emotion', 'empathy', 'Theory of Mind').
source: We used the NeuroSynth meta-analytic database (http://www.neurosynth.org) (Yarkoni et al., 2011) to assess topic terms associated with the training ('attention', 'interoception', 'emotion', 'empathy', 'Theory of Mind').
evidence: This is a description of the method for defining a-priori networks.

claim: The measure for compassion was based on the EmpaToM task, a developed and validated naturalistic video paradigm.
source: The measure for compassion was based on the EmpaToM task, a developed and validated naturalistic video paradigm in the current subjects (Kanske et al., 2015; Tholen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral measure for compassion, supported by citations.

claim: Compassion was quantified as mean of compassion ratings across all experimental conditions.
source: Compassion was quantified as mean of compassion ratings across all experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a description of how compassion was quantified.

claim: The EmpaToM task allowed for measurement of ToM performance through multiple-choice questions requiring inference of mental states.
source: The EmpaToM task (Kanske et al., 2015) also allowed for measurement of ToM performance. After the ratings, multiple-choice questions requiring inference of mental states (thoughts, intentions, beliefs) of the person in the video or factual reasoning on the video's content (control condition) were asked.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral measure for ToM.

claim: Linear mixed-effects models were employed, which allow for inclusion of multiple measurements per subjects and irregular measurement intervals.
source: We employed linear mixed-effects models, a flexible statistical technique that allows for inclusion of multiple measurements per subjects and irregular measurement intervals (Pinheiro and Bates, 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis method.

claim: In all models, age and sex were controlled for, and random effect of subject was included.
source: In all models, we controlled for age and sex, and random effect of subject.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical model covariates.

claim: Findings were corrected for number of tests within the analysis step using FDR correction.
source: Findings were corrected for number of tests within the analysis step using FDR correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This is a description of the multiple comparison correction method.

claim: A supervised framework with cross-validation was adopted to predict behavioral change based on change in functional and microstructural organization within five a-priori functional networks.
source: We adopted a supervised framework with cross-validation to predict behavioral change based on change in functional and microstructural organization within five a-priori functional networks.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral prediction analysis method.

claim: Fivefold cross-validation was utilized separating training and test data and repeated 100 times with different sets of training and test data to avoid bias.
source: We utilized fivefold cross-validation separating training and test data and repeated this procedure 100 times with different sets of training and test data to avoid bias for separating subjects.
